dataTransformationDescription:
## Download the source data

The IMF publishes the World Economic Outlook in April and October. Each new release
is downloaded from the IMF's data API and replaces the previous copy, so the data
reflects the IMF's latest release.

## Select indicators

WEO covers national accounts, prices, employment, the balance of payments, government
finance and commodity prices. The indicators included cover gross domestic product
(GDP), gross national savings, gross capital formation and the output gap.

## Standardise countries and country groups

Country and country group codes are standardised to Data Commons IDs used across the
platform, so data can be compared across datasets. Country groups include the world,
regions and the euro area.

## Convert to whole units

WEO reports some amounts in billions, which are converted to whole units.

## Select dimensions

Every figure is reported against the year and the country. GDP in a country's own
currency and in US dollars is published as one variable in two units. Where a
country's own currency is the US dollar, the two are the same figure, so only the
US-dollar one is published. GDP at purchasing power parity is a separate variable.
Shares record what they are a share of, GDP or potential GDP, and per-capita figures
are divided by population.

## Mark projections as estimated

WEO includes the IMF's projections for the years after the last year the IMF reports
for each series. These values are marked as estimated, so they are kept apart from
reported values. The purchasing power parity series take the last reported year of GDP
in US dollars. Country groups other than the euro area have no last reported year, so
their values are marked as estimated from the year the release is published. The output
gap is marked as modelled in every year, since potential output is never observed.

dataTransformationDescription:
## Download the source data

The complete CRS file is downloaded from the OECD each time the pipeline runs, and
replaces the previous copy, so the data reflects the OECD's latest release.

## Exclude donor core contributions to multilaterals

The OECD instructs that donor core contributions to multilateral organisations,
reported as ordinary CRS rows flagged `bi_multi = 2`, are excluded to compute
bilateral flows. These contributions are already reported in Members' Total Use of
the Multilateral System, so keeping them would double count.

## Standardise providers and recipients

Provider and recipient codes are standardised to Data Commons IDs used across the
platform, so data can be compared across datasets.

## Select dimensions

Every figure is reported against the year, the provider and the recipient, and four
dimensions from the CRS: type of flow, co-operation modality, type of finance and
purpose code. The CRS describes each activity in far more detail than this, including
project titles, descriptions, channels and policy markers, none of which is carried
through.

## Aggregate totals

Activities sharing the same year, provider, recipient and dimensions are summed.
Commitments, disbursements, net disbursements and grant equivalents are each
aggregated as separate measures. Every figure is reported in US dollars at current
prices.

dataTransformationDescription:
## Download the source data

The OECD publishes DAC1 in April, June, September and December. The complete table is
downloaded from the OECD each time it is republished, and replaces the previous copy,
so the data reflects the OECD's latest release.

## Standardise providers

Provider codes are standardised to Data Commons IDs used across the platform, so data
can be compared across datasets. The totals DAC1 reports for groups of providers, such
as all DAC countries, the G7 and the EU members of the DAC, are kept as providers of
their own.

## Select figures

Only figures in current US dollars are included, not constant US dollars or providers'
own currencies. Amounts received are left out, though net disbursements, which subtract
them, are kept. Where DAC1 reports a grant equivalent under two types of aid, the fuller
of the two is used, and total flows as a share of GNI in grant equivalents are left out,
since they repeat ODA as a share of GNI.

## Convert to whole units

DAC1 reports amounts, GNI and population in millions, which are converted to whole
units.

## Select dimensions

Every figure is reported against the year and the provider. Flows are broken down by
type of aid as DAC1 reports it, and by gross or net disbursements, commitments or grant
equivalents, split into grants and non-grants where DAC1 splits them. Shares record that
they are a share of the provider's GNI. GNI and population are reported about the
provider.

dataTransformationDescription:
## Download the source data

The OECD publishes DAC2A in April, June, September and December. The complete table is
downloaded from the OECD each time it is republished, and replaces the previous copy,
so the data reflects the OECD's latest release.

## Standardise providers and recipients

Provider and recipient codes are standardised to Data Commons IDs used across the
platform, so data can be compared across datasets. The totals DAC2A reports for groups
of providers, such as all DAC countries, and for groups of recipients, such as regions
and income groups, are kept as providers and recipients of their own. Where two provider
codes name the same organisation and report the same figures, the figures are kept
once.

## Select figures

Only figures in current US dollars are included, not constant US dollars. Only flows to
recipients on Part I of the DAC List, the developing countries eligible for ODA, are
included. Flows to Part II recipients, the countries in transition, were official aid
rather than ODA, though DAC2A reports them under the same types of aid.

## Convert to whole units

DAC2A reports amounts in millions, which are converted to whole units. ODA per person
and ODA as a share of GNI are kept as reported.

## Select dimensions

Every figure is reported against the year, the provider and the recipient. DAC2A is a
table of disbursements, so every flow is recorded as a disbursement, and its type of aid
says which line of the table it is, such as grants, repayments, interest received, or
debt forgiven or rescheduled. Each flow is counted gross or net as DAC1 counts lines of
the same kind. Repayments, interest received, recoveries and the offsetting entry for debt
relief are net. Grants and rescheduled debt are gross. A flow is marked as neither where
DAC2A does not say which. DAC2A reports total ODA, and ODA loans and other
long-term capital, gross under one type of aid and net under another. Each pair is
published under a single type of aid, with the gross and the net figure told apart by
their netting basis alone. Flows are split into grants and non-grants where the type of
aid is wholly one or the other. Imputed multilateral ODA, the OECD's estimate of each
provider's share of multilateral organisations' ODA, is marked as modelled. Net ODA as a
share of the recipient's GNI records that it is a share of GNI, and net ODA per person
that it is divided by the recipient's population.

## 2026-10-01 First release

### Added

- ONE Conversion Tables (DAC) and ONE Conversion Tables (IMF), each with an exchange rate per US dollar
  about each currency's node and a US-dollar deflator about each country, rebased to equal 100 in the
  declared base year, 2024. The DAC table takes its deflators and donor-currency rates from DAC1 and
  every other currency's rate from the WEO. The IMF table takes both from the WEO. Both tables mark
  values computed from IMF projections with `measurementMethod: IMFProjection`.
- The DAC table fills WEO rates per currency, so a currency DAC1 reports has no rate in the years DAC1
  lacks. Before 1999 its euro rate is EU Institutions' ECU rate, while donors' DAC1 euro amounts are
  legacy currencies at the fixed conversion rates, so each donor's own currency reproduces the OECD's
  national-currency amounts from 1999.
dataTransformationDescription:
## What these tables hold

The graph stores every monetary observation once, in the currency its source reports and at current
prices. The ONE conversion tables hold what it takes to convert those values to another currency or to
constant prices: an exchange rate for each currency and a US-dollar deflator for each country. There are
two tables, each its own import under its own provenance.

- ONE Conversion Tables (DAC) serves OECD data such as the CRS. Its deflators and the rates of the DAC
  donors' currencies come from the OECD DAC1 table, and every other currency's rate comes from the IMF
  World Economic Outlook (WEO).
- ONE Conversion Tables (IMF) serves IMF and World Bank data. Both its rates and its deflators come from
  the WEO.

Each table is computed by its own models and checked by its own tests, so a DAC1 problem, such as a new
donor with no node or a failing DAC check, stops the DAC table and leaves the IMF table to publish. The DAC
table reads the IMF table's rates to fill the currencies DAC1 lacks, so a failure in those rates stops
both.

Each table has two StatVars. The exchange rate is in units of a currency per US dollar, as an annual
average, and each observation is about the currency's node, such as `CurrencyEUR`. The US dollar is 1 in
every year. The deflator is about a country, about EU Institutions, or, in the DAC table, about
`DACCountriesTotal`, and each series equals 100 in the base year the provenance declares as
`deflatorBaseYear`. A value V in currency S, year t, converts to currency T at constant prices of base
year b as V × (D[R, b] / D[R, t]) × X[T, b] / X[S, t], where X is the rate, D the deflator and R the
entity whose prices apply.

## Read the sources

The DAC table reads total net official development assistance (ODA) from DAC1, aid type 1010 and net
disbursements 1140, in current US dollars, in constant US dollars of the DAC base year and in national
currency. The same aid type and flow in each price basis means the ratio of any two is a price or
currency ratio. DAC1 group totals, which carry codes of 20000 and above, are
dropped, except DAC Countries, Total, which becomes `DACCountriesTotal`. Every other donor resolves to its
node through the ontology's DAC code, and a donor with no node fails the build.

Both tables read GDP in national currency (NGDP) and GDP in US dollars (NGDPD) from the WEO, and the
IMF table also reads the GDP deflator (NGDP_D), each flagged as reported or projected by the WEO's last
actual year for that country and series. The WEO staging model stages NGDP_D beside the indicators the
WEO import publishes, and the import leaves it out.

## Compute each area's implied rate

Every area's own rate is computed first. A DAC1 donor's is its national-currency ODA over its US-dollar
ODA. A WEO country's is its national-currency GDP over its US-dollar GDP, and is a projection when either
GDP figure is.

Each area takes the currency the IMF's primary domestic currency map gives its country. The map is
present-tense, so one currency applies to every year. EU Institutions, which have no country, take the
euro from the `currency_rate_reference` seed. A DAC1 donor with no currency, such as DAC Countries,
Total, has no rate.

## Choose one rate per currency

Several areas can share a currency, so `currency_rate_reference` names the area whose rate is the
currency's rate. In the DAC table the euro comes from EU Institutions, which report in euros (ECU before
1999) in every year. In the IMF table it comes from Germany, because the WEO publishes no euro-area GDP in
euros. A currency's issuer supplies it where there is one, as the United States does for the US dollar.
For the CFA francs and the Eastern Caribbean dollar, which no country issues, the seed names a member. A
currency one area uses takes that area's rate. A shared currency with no reference fails the build.

## Check the members agree

Every other member of a shared currency is compared with the reference in the member's last actual year.
Earlier years can sit in a legacy currency, such as a euro member's before it joined, and projected years
follow each country's own forecast, so the latest reported year is the one the present-tense map speaks
for. Members must agree within a relative 1e-6. DAC1's bulk file carries national-currency amounts to six
decimals and real members agree within 1e-8, so 1e-6 leaves headroom while catching a wrong currency. A
member that disagrees beyond the tolerance fails the build. The seed lists the members left out and why:
Andorra and Nauru, whose WEO GDP ratios differ from Germany's and Australia's; Tuvalu, whose GDP the WEO
publishes to the nearest thousand, too coarse for 1e-6; and Bulgaria, which DAC1 reports in lev through 2025
although the map gives the euro it adopted in 2026.

## Fill the DAC table's other currencies

DAC1 publishes rates for its donors' currencies only. The DAC table takes the IMF table's rate for every
other currency, so aid to Kenya converts to Kenyan shillings.

The fill is per currency. A currency DAC1 reports keeps DAC1's rates alone and has no rate in the years
DAC1 lacks: the years after DAC1's latest, which include every WEO projection year, and the years before
its donor began reporting. No currency's series mixes the two sources.

From 1999 each donor's own currency reproduces the OECD's national-currency amounts. Before 1999 the euro
rate is EU Institutions' ECU rate, while donors' DAC1 euro amounts are their legacy currencies converted
at the fixed euro conversion rates, so a donor's pre-1999 euro amounts differ from its US-dollar amounts
converted at the table's euro rate.

The CFP franc and the Caribbean guilder have no source row in either table.

## Check the rates against each other

DAC1 and the WEO compute each currency's rate from independent figures. For every currency-year both
report, the DAC1 rate must lie within a factor of two of the WEO's reported rate. The two differ by
averaging method and fiscal years by far less than a power of ten, so a ratio outside the band means one side
read its amounts at the wrong scale. The US dollar must equal 1 in both. The band guards the rates DAC1
supplies, so it gates the DAC table alone. The DAC member agreement check gates the DAC table alone,
and the IMF member agreement check gates both tables, because the DAC table fills from the IMF rates.

## Compute the US-dollar deflators

A US-dollar deflator moves with domestic prices and the exchange rate together, so converting a
current-dollar value at it gives constant dollars of the base year.

- DAC: 100 × current-dollar ODA / constant-dollar ODA, the deflator the DAC itself applies, for every
  donor and for DAC Countries, Total.
- IMF: NGDP_D × NGDPD / NGDP for each country, which turns the WEO's national-currency deflator into
  US-dollar terms. A value is a projection when any of the three figures is.

## Rebase to the standard base year

Each entity's deflator series is divided by its own value in the base year, so every series equals 100
there. A rebase leaves every ratio of two years, and so every converted value, unchanged. An entity with
no deflator in the base year is left out, because the DAC never rebases a donor that has stopped
reporting and such a series has no known base. The DAC recipe deflates those donors' rows by
`DACCountriesTotal`.

The base year is a pipeline parameter, set to the base year of the DAC's published constant prices. A
test reads the DAC Countries, Total deflator as DAC1 publishes it, before rebasing, and fails the build
unless it equals 100 in the parameter year. When the DAC moves its base year and the parameter lags, the
build fails.

## Mark projections

A rate or deflator computed from an IMF projection carries `measurementMethod: IMFProjection`, in the
same file as the reported values. DAC1 values are all reported.

citation: ONE (2026), ONE Conversion Tables (IMF), https://docs.one.org/methodologies/data/oda/currency-conversion/ (accessed on 2026-10-02), computed from IMF, World Economic Outlook, https://data.imf.org/en/datasets/IMF.RES:WEO

## 2026-09-21 First release

### Added

- Dataset added to the graph: imputed multilateral spending by sector and recipient, computed from
  `oda-data`'s `imputed_multilateral_by_purpose`. Channels resolve through `oda-data`'s reviewed
  provider/agency crosswalk; a core contribution with no usable share from its own channel falls back to a
  stale window, a reviewed proxy channel, or an explicit `unallocated` status published against DAC
  recipient 9998 and CRS purpose 998. Amounts are gross disbursements at current US dollar prices; both
  source releases (CRS and Members' Total Use) are cited with their own release year. The series are
  `FinancialFlow` StatVars measuring `attributedAmount`, constrained by `dac2aAidType`
  `DAC2aAidType106`, with measurement method `Modelled`.
dataTransformationDescription:
## What this dataset measures

A multilateral organisation pools a provider's core contributions and spends them across sectors and
recipients on its own account. This dataset attributes that spending back to the original provider, in
proportion to its share of each multilateral's core resources, and breaks it down by recipient and by
sector. It answers "how much of a provider's money reached this sector in this recipient country, once its
contributions to multilaterals are spread the way those multilaterals spent them", a question the CRS
alone cannot answer. The CRS records a provider's payment to the multilateral, not what the multilateral
did with it.

This is a different question from a bilateral relationship where the provider is itself a multilateral
organisation, such as IDA disbursing directly to Kenya. That spending is already a CRS row under IDA's own
provider code and is not part of this dataset.

## Download the source data

The pipeline downloads two OECD bulk releases: the Creditor Reporting System (CRS), which supplies the
sector mix each multilateral's spending followed, and Members' Total Use of the Multilateral System, which
supplies each provider's core contributions. Both are read through the `oda-data` package, and both are
fingerprinted by the `-vYYYYMMDD` republish token the OECD attaches to each bulk file. `resolve_bulk_versions`
in `src/dfo_pipelines/defs/one/imputed_multilateral_sectors/assets.py` reads both tokens, and
`one_imputed_multilateral_sectors_source` observes them daily so the pipeline reruns when either changes.

`one_imputed_multilateral_sectors_raw_file` calls `imputed_multilateral_by_purpose` with `refresh=True`, so
every materialization re-reads both releases rather than serving a cached copy. `resolve_bulk_versions` is
called again immediately before and immediately after that compute, and `verify_release_provenance` checks
the compute's own `result.attrs["provenance"]` against the token observed before it, then checks that same
token against the one observed after. The run refuses to write, leaving no parquet file and no metadata,
when `oda-data`'s recorded release disagrees with the token observed before the compute, or when either
source's token moves between the two observations: `oda-data` resolves its own release identity through a
7-day HTTP annotation cache, so it can otherwise report a release that no longer matches what was read.

## Compute the imputed spending

For each provider, `oda-data`'s `imputed_multilateral_by_purpose` function takes the provider's core
contributions to each multilateral and spreads them across sectors and recipients in the same proportions
that multilateral's own CRS-reported spending followed over its current three-year window (`period_length`,
default 3). Those shares are computed over CRS spending flagged Official Development Assistance (ODA) or
Other Official Flows (OOF) combined (`flow_types=("ODA", "OOF")`), because several multilateral channels,
among them IBRD, EBRD, IFC and IDB Invest, report only OOF to the CRS; an ODA-only share basis would leave
those channels with no CRS spending to compute a share from. `flow_types=("ODA", "OOF")` affects only the
CRS spending the shares are computed from, not the core-contribution amounts read from Members' Total Use.
Every value is a gross disbursement at current US dollar prices.

An observation is dated to the year the provider made the contribution, not to the years the underlying
sector mix was drawn from. Because that sector mix comes from the three years up to and including the
contribution year, a value published against year n can change if the CRS is later revised for year n-1 or
n-2, even though the contribution itself did not change. Re-running the pipeline against a revised CRS
vintage updates the affected years' values, and nothing in the observation itself records that it moved.

Coverage starts in 2011, the first year Members' Total Use of the Multilateral System reports, even though
the CRS itself runs back to 1973. Every observation is a gross disbursement, so this dataset will not
reconcile against headline grant-equivalent ODA figures, which measure the same flows on a different basis.

## Resolve which channel the money passed through

Each multilateral's CRS spending resolves to a DAC channel code through a crosswalk `oda-data` ships and
maintains under review, keyed on the exact `(provider_code, agency_code)` pair the CRS reports. A
`(provider_code, agency_code)` pair carrying nonzero value with no reviewed row in that crosswalk raises
`UnmappedChannelError` inside `imputed_multilateral_by_purpose`, and nothing in this pipeline catches it: a
new OECD channel appearing in the CRS before it has been reviewed and added to the crosswalk fails the run
loudly.

This dataset ships without a channel dimension. `int_imputed_multilateral_sectors_aggregated.sql` sums over
`channel_code` once entities are resolved, so a user cannot see which multilateral a given amount travelled
through, only the total across all of them for a given provider, recipient, sector and year.

## Allocate every core contribution

Every core contribution `oda-data` reads from Members' Total Use follows exactly one allocation route. A
contribution spread across recipients and purposes gives many output rows, every one of them tagged with
the same `allocation_status` and together summing to the contribution:

- `imputed`: the channel's own CRS spending in its current three-year window produced the share.
- `stale_share`: the channel reported no CRS spending in its current window, so its most recent window with
  data, within `max_share_age` (default 5) years, is used instead.
- `proxy`: a reviewed proxy channel's shares stand in for the channel's own; for example, the Multilateral
  Debt Relief Initiative uses IDA's shares. A fixed purpose code carries no recipient of its own, so a
  fixed-purpose proxy row, for example UN peacekeeping core contributions under purpose code 15230, carries
  a null `recipient_code` instead.
- `unallocated`: no usable share exists, at any age, from the channel itself or a reviewed proxy; both
  `recipient_code` and `purpose_code` are null.

`stg_imputed_multilateral_sectors.sql` keeps rows for all four allocation statuses, so a provider's total
across this dataset always equals its Members' Total Use core contributions. A null `recipient_code`, from a
fixed-purpose proxy row or an `unallocated` row, is published against DAC recipient code 9998, "Bilateral,
unallocated/unspecified"; an `unallocated` row's null `purpose_code` is published against CRS purpose code
998, "Unallocated/unspecified". The `unallocated` share of that year's total core money, reported in
`one_imputed_multilateral_sectors_raw_file`'s materialization metadata under
`unallocated_value_share_by_year`, is a coverage figure over the published values.

[`oda-data` pull request #167](https://github.com/ONEcampaign/oda_data_package/pull/167) measures this
split on CRS release v20260803 and Members' Total Use release v20260710, across 2015-2024: 89.15% of core
money is imputed, 4.04% proxy, 0.21% stale share, and 6.59% unallocated. This pipeline reports those same
four shares for each run in `one_imputed_multilateral_sectors_raw_file`'s materialization metadata.

## Resolve providers and recipients, and select dimensions

Provider and recipient codes are standardised to Data Commons IDs used across the platform, so data can be
compared across datasets. Every figure is reported against the year, the provider, the recipient and the
purpose code. Netting basis, flow type and flow category are constants across the whole dataset (gross
disbursement, ODA) rather than dimensions read from the source, because this is the only combination
`oda-data`'s imputation method produces.

Each series is a `FinancialFlow` StatVar measuring `attributedAmount`, the part of a flow's amount credited
to a provider whose resources it draws on, where the flow cannot be traced to that provider directly. Here
the flow is the multilateral's own spending and the resources are the provider's core contributions. The
StatVar is constrained by `dac2aAidType` `DAC2aAidType106`, which marks this dataset's series,
so its Data Commons IDs differ from those of a CRS series for the same purpose. The IDs order the
constraints `nettingBasis`, `financialFlowType`, `crsTypeOfFlow`, `dac2aAidType`, `crsPurpose`. Every
observation carries `measurementMethod` `Modelled`, since each value is computed from shares.

## Aggregate totals

Activities sharing the same year, provider, recipient and purpose code are summed, across every channel
they passed through. Every figure is reported in US dollars at current prices.

## Cite each source's own release

`dc_imputed_multilateral_sectors_provenance.sql` cites CRS and Members' Total Use separately, each with its
own release year, since the two publish months apart; the leading "ONE (year)" citation uses the later of
the two years. `next_source_release_date` is the earlier of CRS's own next scheduled release, one of April,
June, September or December, and Members' Total Use's next annual release. Members' Total Use derives from
the same CRS activity-level microdata that only becomes final at CRS's December release, so it carries no
April preliminary counterpart the way CRS does, and the pipeline models its own next release as arriving
every December. `next_crs_release_date` and `next_multisystem_release_date`, in `dbt/macros/`, each compute
their own source's next date from its own last observed release date, and
`dc_imputed_multilateral_sectors_provenance.sql` takes the earlier (`least()`) of the two.

## Combining this dataset with the CRS

A provider total built from both this dataset and the CRS counts each core contribution once.
`stg_dac_crs.sql` excludes CRS rows flagged `bi_multi = 2`, the OECD's own flag for a donor's core
contribution to a multilateral organisation, and keeps rows where the flag is null. Members' Total Use
reports the same contributions, and this dataset spreads them across sectors and recipients, so `oecd_dac_crs`
carries a provider's bilateral spending while this dataset carries the redistributed core spending, with no
overlap between the two.

The B02 family of cooperation-modality codes (`B02`, `B021`, `B022`, `B02a`, `B02b`) is only partly mapped in
`code_mapping`: `B02a` and `B02b` have no ontology mapping, so a CRS row reported under either code has no
cooperation-modality segment in its Data Commons ID. The `bi_multi = 2` exclusion removes any double count
between the two datasets, and the unmapped codes are a completeness gap in the cooperation-modality
dimension of the CRS series.

This dataset restates each provider's own contributions rather than adding new recipient-side information.
The question "how much reached this recipient, from all providers combined" is a recipient-perspective
total, and the CRS alone answers it.

dataTransformationDescription:
## Download the source data

The World Bank publishes IDS as six bulk files, split by debtor name. All six are
downloaded each time the pipeline runs, and replace the previous copy, so the data
reflects the World Bank's latest release.

## Exclude series outside the debt statistics

Non-debt statistics are excluded, including population, balance of payments, investment
and reserves. GNI is kept, because some debt ratios are shares of it. Exports of goods,
services and primary income, and the three debt ratios that are shares of it, are
excluded until the ontology can describe them. Debt forgiveness grants, the stock-flow
reconciliation residual, the annual changes in debt stocks and interest arrears, and the
present value of debt are also excluded.

## Omit zeros where no lending took place

IDS reports a value for every debtor, creditor and series, including pairs with no
lending between them, so most figures are zero. Zeros are kept on world totals, and
within or after a period of lending between a debtor and a creditor. They are omitted
where a creditor has not lent to a debtor, for the years before lending began, and for
averages in years with no new commitments, since there is nothing to average.

## Standardise debtors and creditors

Debtor and creditor codes are standardised to Data Commons IDs used across the
platform, so data can be compared across datasets. Where a series names a single lender
in its code, such as debt owed to the IBRD, that lender becomes the creditor.

## Select dimensions

Every figure is reported against the year, the debtor and the creditor, and the
dimensions the World Bank encodes in each series code, such as type of flow, maturity
and creditor type. GNI is the exception: it describes the debtor economy, so it is
reported against the year and the economy alone. Ratios record what they are a share of:
GNI or total external debt stocks. Every amount is reported in US dollars at current
prices.

## Mark projections as estimated

For the years after the last reported year, the World Bank projects debt service and
disbursements on commitments already made. These values are marked as estimated, so
they are kept apart from reported values.
